chunks: "The Fourier Transform is a way of rewriting a signal in terms of frequency instead of time.

The idea is that almost any signal can be built as a sum, or integral, of sine waves of different frequencies, amplitudes and phases, and the transform tells you how much of each frequency is in the signal.
Mathematically, X(f) equals the integral of x(t)e to the -j2 pi ft dt .
You multiply the signal by a complex sinusoid at frequency f and integrate, which measures how well the signal correlates with that frequency.
The magnitude of X(f) is the amplitude at that frequency, and the angle is the phase.
The inverse transform sums those sinusoids back up to reconstruct the signal, so no information is lost.

Why it matters to a hardware engineer: for linear circuits, each frequency passes through independently, so the output spectrum is just the input spectrum times the circuit's frequency response, which is exactly what a Bode plot shows.
Convolution in the time domain becomes simple multiplication in the frequency domain.
It also explains things like why a sharp edge has a lot of high-frequency content, so a one nanosecond rise time needs about 350 megahertz of bandwidth.
And in practice we compute it with the FFT, which is how scopes and spectrum analyzers show you the harmonics and noise of a signal."
